clinicalPearls: The pituitary manifestation of systemic IgG4-related disease, an immune-mediated fibroinflammatory condition
Presents with anterior hypopituitarism and/or central diabetes insipidus, together with mass-effect symptoms such as headache and visual disturbance from a pituitary or stalk mass
More common in older men, often with evidence of IgG4-related disease elsewhere such as autoimmune pancreatitis, sialadenitis, retroperitoneal fibrosis or orbital disease
MRI shows pituitary enlargement and/or a thickened stalk that may mimic other inflammatory or neoplastic sellar lesions
Serum IgG4 is often but not always elevated, so diagnosis integrates histology, imaging, serology and other organ involvement
Where histology is obtained it shows a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate rich in IgG4-positive plasma cells, storiform fibrosis and sometimes obliterative phlebitis
It typically responds well to glucocorticoid therapy with shrinkage of the mass, though hormone deficits may persist and relapse can occur
Recognised diagnostic criteria help distinguish it from other forms of hypophysitis
reference.pathophysiology: IgG4-related hypophysitis is the pituitary expression of systemic IgG4-related disease, a fibroinflammatory disorder in which affected tissues are infiltrated by IgG4-positive plasma cells and lymphocytes, with storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis. In the sella this infiltrate expands and later fibroses the anterior pituitary and infundibulum, impairing hormone secretion and disrupting antidiuretic hormone pathways, producing variable anterior hypopituitarism and central diabetes insipidus together with a space-occupying mass. The underlying immunopathogenesis involves aberrant T-helper, including T-follicular-helper, and regulatory responses driving class switching to IgG4 and tissue fibrosis, and the condition commonly coexists with IgG4-related involvement of other organs.
additionalDifferentials: Granulomatous hypophysitis and other primary hypophysitides
Sarcoidosis or tuberculosis of the pituitary or stalk
Langerhans cell histiocytosis causing stalk thickening
Pituitary adenoma or other sellar neoplasm
Germinoma or metastasis presenting as a stalk lesion
additionalInvestigations: Pituitary MRI showing gland enlargement and/or stalk thickening, with loss of the posterior bright spot in diabetes insipidus
Serum IgG4 concentration, supportive if raised but neither sensitive nor specific
Full anterior pituitary hormone assessment and evaluation of posterior pituitary function with paired plasma and urine osmolality, and water deprivation testing where needed
Screening for IgG4-related disease elsewhere with imaging of the pancreas, salivary glands and retroperitoneum, and biopsy of an accessible organ if present
Pituitary biopsy with IgG4 immunostaining in diagnostically uncertain cases
Exclusion of alternative infiltrative or neoplastic causes as clinically indicated
redFlags: Acute visual field loss or ophthalmoplegia from mass effect
Adrenal insufficiency from ACTH deficiency, with a risk of crisis
Rapid enlargement or atypical features suggesting malignancy and requiring biopsy
reference.prognosis: Generally favourable; the mass and inflammation usually respond to glucocorticoid therapy with radiological improvement, but established hormone deficits including diabetes insipidus often persist and require replacement, and relapse may necessitate further immunosuppression.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for a pituitary adenoma and proceeding to unnecessary surgery when it may respond to glucocorticoids
Relying on a normal serum IgG4 to exclude the diagnosis
Overlooking systemic IgG4-related disease in other organs
Failing to recognise and replace cortisol deficiency before it precipitates a crisis
references: Diagnostic criteria for IgG4-related hypophysitis (Leporati et al.)
management: Induce remission with glucocorticoids, which usually shrink the sellar mass and may partially restore pituitary function
Replace deficient anterior pituitary hormones, ensuring glucocorticoid cover is established before thyroxine, and add sex-steroid or growth-hormone replacement as needed
Treat central diabetes insipidus with desmopressin, as this deficit often persists
Monitor with serial pituitary MRI, formal visual field assessment and repeat hormone profiling
Use steroid-sparing immunosuppression or rituximab for relapse or steroid dependence
Screen for IgG4-related disease in other organs such as the pancreas, salivary glands and retroperitoneum
Manage through endocrinology, reserving neurosurgery for compressive disease unresponsive to medical therapy
